2.0.s.en: 1. The inner preparation for the building

2.0.0.en: 1 And Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. 2 And Solomon told out threescore and ten thousand men to bear burdens, and fourscore thousand to hew in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred to oversee them.

2.0.1.en: Solomon presents to us a method of building, whether spiritual or temporal, which is to begin with the inside before a person asks about his needs from outside.

2.0.2.en: And Solomon determined to build an house for the name of the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. [1]

2.0.3.en: Solomon issued his order to build a house for the name of the Lord, and also to build the royal palace. It is noticeable in this order that he proclaims the priority of the house of the Lord, and at the same time does not ignore the needs of the state, that is, building a palace to manage the affairs of the state. Spiritual work does not mean laxity or neglect or ignoring temporal obligations and responsibilities. Moreover, he did not ask for a house for his personal comfort and to display his greatness, but asked for a house for his kingdom, that is, to serve the state, to receive his subjects, and to be an honor to the state among the other states. It is as though the first house is for the glory of God, and the second for the common good. He does not seek what is for himself, but rather what is for the Lord and for his brethren.

2.0.4.en: The original Hebrew text says: “and a royal house for him”, used for administering the kingdom and as a palace for his dwelling. This palace required high-level planning; the planning and building took about thirteen years (1 Kgs 7:1-12).

2.0.5.en: Solomon inherited from his father the longings of his heart, and fulfilled what David used to dream of, as he sang, saying: “One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple” (Ps 27:4).

2.0.6.en: [I will not enter the tabernacle of my house, nor go up into my bed, I will not give slumber to mine eyes, nor sleep to mine eyelids, until I find out a place for the LORD, an habitation for the mighty God of Jacob] (Ps 132:3-5).

2.0.7.en: In the wilderness the people used to bring offerings and sacrifices to the movable tabernacle, and now that they had settled in the Promised Land, and the prophet David had made huge efforts to expand the kingdom, the time had come for the house of the Lord to be built, especially since David had prepared much material and many designs, and had made the leaders and the people ready for the work.

2.1.0.en: And Solomon told out threescore and ten thousand men to bear burdens, and fourscore thousand to hew in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred to oversee them. [2]

2.1.1.en: Some see that the personality of Solomon differs from that of his father David: David was the simple shepherd who loved the people of God and served them with all his heart, while Solomon was the man famous for the wisdom given to him by God to set up buildings, especially the temple of God.

2.1.2.en: David was the military commander who was occupied with battles from his youth on behalf of the people of God, relying on God, the Giver of victory. Solomon, however, was the man of politics, who tried to win the nations around him, that they might support him in carrying out his projects.

2.1.3.en: David was the ideal leader, who did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, so that he was counted the standard by which every king of Judah was evaluated; Solomon, on the other hand, was ideal in his wisdom, and his credit is that he built the temple (Jn 10:23; Acts 3:11; 5:12), which the Jews to this day long to rebuild.

2.1.4.en: Some see that Solomon thought he had elevated his people, as he brought them into the family of the nations, and entered into commercial treaties that brought prosperity and glory to his people in his days. But the cost was heavy and bitter after his death and for long generations, for his policy caused his people to decline spiritually.

2.2.s.en: 2. He asks the king of Tyre for a skilled man

2.2.0.en: 3 And Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying, As thou didst deal with David my father, and didst send him cedars to build him an house to dwell therein, 4 Behold, I build an house to the name of the LORD my God, to dedicate it to him, and to burn before him sweet incense, and for the continual shewbread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the LORD our God. This is an ordinance for ever to Israel. 5 And the house which I build is great: for great is our God above all gods. 6 But who is able to build him an house, seeing the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him? who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him? 7 Send me now therefore a man cunning to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, and in iron, and in purple, and crimson, and blue, and that can skill to grave with the cunning men that are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father did provide.

2.2.1.en: And Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying,

2.2.2.en: As thou didst deal with David my father, and didst send him cedars to build him an house to dwell therein [3]

2.2.3.en: After Solomon had numbered the men working in his state, he turned to the king of Tyre in a spiritual, gentle and wise manner.

2.2.4.en: Solomon sent to Huram, perhaps to thank him for his congratulations on his enthronement as king, and at the same time to ask for his help in building a temple for the Lord. Here we note the following:

2.2.5.en: a. He begins his message by revealing the good relations that existed between Huram, king of Tyre, and his father David, as though his own relationship went back to an old and genuine friendship without a blemish [3]. David had spoken with Hiram about building the house of the Lord and about the covenant with God (1 Kgs 7). So Solomon asked the king of Tyre for a sign of the development of a genuine friendship marked by affection.

2.2.6.en: b. He is not setting up a memorial monument for his father, but building a temple for God, whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain. What occupied Solomon was neither his own temporal glory nor the glory of his father, but the glory of the living God.

2.2.7.en: c. With some clarity Solomon reveals to Huram his purpose in building the house of the Lord his God, namely that the people, with their priests, may practice the following:

2.3.0.en: · To dedicate it to Him [4], that is, to bear witness to Him that He is holy, imitating the Seraphim when they say “Holy” three times (Isa 6:3), repeating it without ceasing.

2.3.1.en: · To burn before Him sweet incense [4], imitating the living creatures and the heavenly elders who stand before the Lamb, each of whom has harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev 5:8)

2.3.3.en: · To offer burnt offerings morning and evening [4].

2.3.4.en: · To observe weekly feasts (the sabbaths), monthly feasts (the new moons), and yearly feasts (the solemn feasts of the Lord our God), besides the Jubilee, etc. [4].

2.3.5.en: In his friendship with the king of Tyre he does not flatter, but bears witness to God: “for great is our God above all gods... the heaven of heavens cannot contain him [5-6]. Solomon feared that Hiram would think that the God of Israel is like his pagan gods, whom they confine in their temples.

2.4.0.en: c. While taking pride in God in humility, he writes without shame: “Who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him?! [6]. Although he desires to build a great house, there is no basis of comparison between the greatness of the house and the greatness of the Lord Himself. He wanted to assure the king that God is not like the gods of the nations, dwelling in temples made with hands (Acts 17:24). Rather, he builds the house so that the priests and worshippers may find a place in which they express their love for God and their desire to worship Him.

2.4.1.en: d. What Solomon asks is that Huram supply him with a wise, experienced leader. For Solomon has skilled men in Jerusalem and Judah, whom his father David had previously appointed (1 Chr 22:15), and he needs a leader who can lead these skilled men.

2.4.2.en: The king of Tyre represented the Gentiles whom the people had not succeeded in driving out or enslaving, but he represents the few who could accept faith in God, and these were accepted as partners in this great work: erecting a house for the Lord.

2.4.3.en: Solomon's letter to Huram, king of Tyre, reveals the biblical view of the temple, or the house of the Lord.

2.4.4.en: First: The book, especially this letter, reveals that the main work of King Solomon is building the temple and organizing worship in it, and the whole nation's being occupied with meeting God through worship. It seems as though Solomon, with his wisdom and his activities, has nothing but this temple.

2.4.5.en: Second: The affirmation that God is not limited to any place, and that God declares His presence for the sake of His people, that they may enjoy meeting Him, and the expression of the mutual love between God and humanity, especially His people.

2.4.6.en: Third: Solomon's concern for the contribution of Huram and his men in building the temple is considered the way to reveal the calling of the Gentiles to the Gospel of Christ. This was a matter that God was preparing the Jews to accept throughout their whole history and through their prophets.

2.4.7.en: For Job was found, who was not of the seed of Abraham, and one of the books of the Holy Bible is recorded in his name. It was also said of him: “That man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1).

2.4.8.en: And the divine promise came to Abraham himself: “As for me, behold, my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations” (Gen 17:4).

2.4.9.en: The Lord says: “Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called an house of prayer for all people” (Isa 56:7).

2.4.10.en: v “No prophet is accepted in his own country” (Lk 4:24). Since Anathoth was the homeland of Jeremiah (Jer 11:21), it did not receive him well. Likewise Isaiah and the rest of the prophets were rejected by the children of their homeland, that is, the people of the circumcision... But we, who do not belong to the covenant but were strangers to the promise, received Moses and the prophets who proclaim Christ, we received them with all our hearts more than the Jews, who rejected Christ and did not accept the testimony to Him[1].

2.5.0.en: Behold, I build an house to the name of the LORD my God, to dedicate it to him, and to burn before him sweet incense, and for the continual shewbread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the sabbaths, and on the new moons, and on the solemn feasts of the LORD our God.

2.5.1.en: This is an ordinance for ever to Israel. [4]

2.5.2.en: King Solomon explained the meaning of erecting the temple to Huram in a way that differs from what is stated in the Book of Kings, and Solomon brought out the concept of the house of the Lord: 1. The house of God in which He dwells in the midst of His people [3), that is, it represents the divine presence. 2. The personal house of God with every believer: “to the name of the LORD my God” [4]. 3. The house of holiness in which the fragrance of sweet incense rises [4]. When he says: “to dedicate it to him”, he invites us to imitate the Seraphim whom the prophet Isaiah saw, who says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Above it stood the seraphims: each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly. And one cried to another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, LORD of hosts, his glory is the fulness of all the earth” (Isa 6:1-3). St. Cyril the Great has wonderful comments on this text touching our obligation to the holy life and the holy worship that befits being offered to the holy God.

2.5.3.en: v They fly, since they have nothing to weigh them down and bring them low. Their minds are always lifted up toward God; their authority is in the heights, they do not contemplate the things below, as we do, but keep their minds on the ineffable heavenly thoughts.

2.5.4.en: Their mouths offer praise; they confess in turn in order without weariness, as I see it, but in a manner that allows others to offer honors of praise in hymns of thanksgiving, since everything in the heights is carried out in exact order...

2.5.5.en: They say “Holy” three times, and conclude the hymn of praise with the Lord Sabaoth, thus pointing to the Holy Trinity of one divine nature.

2.5.6.en: In our confession we say that the Father exists, and so do the Son and the Holy Spirit. There is no difference in nature to distinguish between these, but one divinity perceived in three hypostases. This is confirmed to us by the holy Seraphim themselves, who say that the whole earth is full of His glory, having foretold in advance the future mystery of the Incarnation of Christ.

2.5.7.en: Before the Word became flesh, in truth Satan the avenger, the dragon, the apostate, ruled the earth under heaven, and creation was worshipped instead of the Creator who made it. But when the Word became flesh, all the earth was filled with His glory, and every knee bows to Him and every tribe and tongue confesses and serves Him, as the Holy Scripture says.

2.5.8.en: The blessed David offered that cry beforehand in the Spirit, saying: “All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Ps 86:9; Phil 2:10-11)[2].

2.5.9.en: St. Cyril the Great 4. The house of the continual heavenly table, “for the continual shewbread”. 5. The house of perfect love, in which the believer offers all his life as a perfect burnt offering night and day. Solomon referred to the burnt offerings and did not refer to the sin offering or the trespass offering, for the book here does not speak of sins and their forgiveness, but transports us as if into heaven itself, where there is continual praise and burnt offerings of perfect love. 6. The house of continual joy, for celebrating the sabbaths, the new moons, and the solemn feasts of the LORD our God [4]. By the feasts of the Lord he means the great yearly feasts, which are the Passover, the Feast of Weeks (Pentecost), and the Feast of Tabernacles (Lev 23:4-44; Deut 16:1-17).

2.6.0.en: And the house which I build is great: for great is our God above all gods. [5]

2.7.0.en: But who is able to build him an house?

2.7.1.en: seeing the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain him? who am I then, that I should build him an house, save only to burn sacrifice before him? [6]

2.7.2.en: The Old Testament often spoke of the heaven of heavens (Deut 10:14; 1 Kgs 8:27; 2 Chr 6:18; Neh 9:6; Ps 68:33; Ps 148:4).

2.7.3.en: The Apostle Paul says of himself that he “was caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor 12:2).

2.7.4.en: It is stated in the Targum: [For the lower heavens and the middle heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain Him, since He is the One who upholds all things with His arm by His authority. Heaven is the throne of His glory, and the earth the footstool of His feet, the deep and the whole world are supported by the Spirit of His word... So who am I that I should build Him a house?[3]]

2.7.5.en: The Jews believed in the existence of seven heavens, and the Old Testament speaks of “the heaven of heavens”, by which is often meant the third heaven, where the divine throne is and the dwelling of the saints with the heavenly ones in eternal life. Some, like Ambrosiaster, see that St. Paul was caught up twice, once to the third heaven, and again to Paradise, to which the right-hand thief went when the Lord Christ was crucified.

2.8.0.en: Send me now therefore a man cunning to work in gold, and in silver, and in brass, and in iron, and in purple, and crimson, and blue, and that can skill to grave with the cunning men that are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father did provide. [7]

2.8.1.en: Archaeological remains and excavations have proved that the Israelites were not experts in the arts.

2.8.2.en: If God chose the children of Israel of old as a people for Himself, it was only to prepare the way so that the Savior of the world might come from the tribe of Judah, opening the gates of heaven to all nations and peoples. It is said in Isaiah: “And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls, and their kings shall minister unto thee... Therefore thy gates shall be open continually; they shall not be shut day nor night; that the wealth of the Gentiles may be brought unto thee, and that their kings may be led” (Isa 60:10-11). And it is said in Zechariah: “And they that are far off shall come and build in the temple of the LORD, and ye shall know that the LORD of hosts hath sent me unto you” (Zech 6:15).

2.8.3.en: Solomon opens the gates of heaven to the peoples and nations, for the house that is built for God, whom the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain, will it be limited to a particular people? It is the house of God, the Creator of heaven and earth, where He is pleased by the gathering of all peoples with Him and with His servants the heavenly orders.

2.9.s.en: 3. He asks for the best kinds of wood

2.9.0.en: Send me also cedar trees, fir trees, and algum trees, out of Lebanon: for I know that thy servants can skill to cut timber in Lebanon;

2.9.1.en: and, behold, my servants shall be with thy servants, [8]

2.10.0.en: And let them prepare me timber in abundance: for the house which I build is great and wonderful. [9]

2.10.1.en: Just as he asked him for a man who would be great in his skill and administration, so he also asked that the materials used to erect the house of the Lord be of the best kinds, “for the house which I build is great and wonderful” [9].

2.11.s.en: 4. The pledge to provide for the workers

2.11.0.en: And, behold, I will give to the hewers that cut timber twenty thousand measures of wheat as food for thy servants, and twenty thousand measures of barley, and twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil. [10]

2.11.1.en: King Solomon pledges that he will be very generous in providing for the workers. Solomon assured Huram that he does not offer the workers “bread and water” but enough and more than enough of wheat, barley, wine and oil. What concerns him is not only to give them good wages, but he also cares for their nourishment and comfort, since he offers them “wine”.

2.11.2.en: Barley, wine and ordinary oil used to be given as food to foreign workers[4].

2.12.s.en: 5. The letter of the king of Tyre to him

2.12.0.en: 11 Then Huram the king of Tyre said in a writing which he sent to Solomon, Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them. 12 Huram said moreover, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth, who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding, who builds an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. 13 And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding, Huram my father, 14 The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre, skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father. 15 Now therefore the wheat, and the barley, the oil, and the wine, which my lord hath spoken of, let him send unto his servants: 16 And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in flotes by sea to Joppa; and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem.

2.12.1.en: Then Huram the king of Tyre said in a writing which he sent to Solomon,

2.12.2.en: Because the LORD hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them. [11]

2.12.3.en: Solomon's style, full of wisdom and dignity and honor toward the king of Tyre, had its effect on Huram, so he wrote to him congratulating the people of Israel on their wise king: “Because the LORD... hath loved his people, he hath made thee king over them” [11]. He did not say that because the Lord loves you He made you king, but “because the LORD hath loved his people”. Good leaders are a great gift that God gives to the holy people who are beloved of God.

2.12.4.en: Huram's answer to Solomon's letter reveals the spread of the knowledge of the Lord among the nations, and also suggests the response of the Gentiles to the Gospel of Christ and their delight in it. We may say that Huram here prepared the way, symbolically, for the Church of the Gentiles.

2.12.5.en: First: Huram, king of Tyre, played the role of Cornelius, the Gentile commander, and his household, whom he gathered in his house to meet Simon Peter, to listen to him, and to enjoy baptism.

2.12.6.en: Second: This work paves the way for what the Apostle Paul did in his concern for ministering to the people of the uncircumcision, or the Gentiles, and their response to his preaching. Huram's answer befits the Gentiles who thirst to know the Gospel truth and to believe in it[5].

2.13.0.en: Huram said moreover, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth, who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding, who builds an house for the LORD, and an house for his kingdom. [12]

2.13.1.en: Huram bore witness that the Lord loved His people, in that He made Solomon king over them, because he is the wise son of David, endued with knowledge, who builds a house for the Lord and a house for his kingdom. Is there not in this a prophecy, in the Gentiles' testimony to the true Solomon, the Lord of glory, the Son of David, who is the wisdom of God, who built the Church of the New Testament as an eternal house, the center of His heavenly kingdom?!

2.13.2.en: The king of Tyre looks on Solomon not only as a good gift from the Lord to His people, but also as a good gift to his father David: “who hath given to David the king a wise son, endued with knowledge and understanding” [12]. A wise and understanding son is a gift from God to his family.

2.13.3.en: It is clear from the style of King Huram that he had come to know the living God through his relationship with David as well as from the letter of his son Solomon, for he wrote: “Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, that made heaven and earth” [12].

2.13.4.en: The people of Israel walked in a spirit of godliness and uprightness, thanks to the godliness and conduct of David, which had its effect on neighboring peoples such as Tyre. Conversely, when the people worshipped the gods of the neighboring nations, at the same time these nations rose against them, defeated them and humiliated them. When man flatters evil, evil itself destroys him and takes away his dignity and his potential.

2.14.0.en: And now I have sent a cunning man, endued with understanding, (named) Huram my father [13]

2.14.1.en: Huram my father: in the original, Huram Abi. The word “father” here does not mean the father of the king; rather it is a title of honor for the chief or master of the workmen, who bears toward them a kind of fatherhood[6].

2.15.0.en: (The son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man of Tyre)

2.15.1.en: skilful to work in gold, and in silver, in brass, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, and in fine linen, and in crimson; also to grave any manner of graving, and to find out every device which shall be put to him, with thy cunning men, and with the cunning men of my lord David thy father. [14]

2.15.2.en: He sent to him a wise man in whose veins ran Israelite and Gentile blood, for his mother was of the daughters of Dan[7], and his father was a Tyrian. This wise man points to the Church of the New Testament, which includes members of Jewish origin alongside members of Gentile origin.

2.16.0.en: Now therefore the wheat, and the barley, the oil, and the wine, which my lord hath spoken of, let him send unto his servants: [15]

2.17.0.en: And we will cut wood out of Lebanon, as much as thou shalt need: and we will bring it to thee in flotes by sea to Joppa;

2.17.1.en: and thou shalt carry it up to Jerusalem. [16]

2.17.2.en: A treaty was concluded between the two kings: the king of Tyre provides Solomon with all his needs, and brings them to Joppa, and Solomon provides all the needs of the workers [15-16]. This treaty is mentioned in (1 Kgs 5:8-9).

2.18.s.en: 6. The partnership of the foreigners in the work

2.18.0.en: 17 And Solomon numbered all the strangers that were in the land of Israel, after the numbering wherewith David his father had numbered them; and they were found an hundred and fifty thousand and three thousand and six hundred. 18 And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work.

2.18.1.en: And Solomon numbered all the strangers that were in the land of Israel, after the numbering wherewith David his father had numbered them; and they were found an hundred and fifty thousand and three thousand and six hundred. [17]

2.18.2.en: By the strangers he means the Canaanites who dwelt in the land of old and whom the children of Israel did not drive out.

2.19.0.en: And he set threescore and ten thousand of them to be bearers of burdens, and fourscore thousand to be hewers in the mountain, and three thousand and six hundred overseers to set the people a work. [18]

2.19.1.en: Solomon employed the strangers, who had no right of inheritance in the Promised Land, as bearers of burdens and cutters of stone, and their number at that time was large, reaching one hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred. He did not employ them for forced labor, but that they might earn their living generously, for the commandment came: [Thou shalt not oppress a stranger](*).

2.19.2.en: Besides the good things Canaan had because of its fertile land, the project of building the temple was huge, and many benefited from it. This was besides the building of the royal palace and other projects he undertook.

2.19.3.en: What do You want me to do, O Lord?

2.19.4.en: v You chose David the boy, the youngest of his brothers.

2.19.5.en: His father and his brothers despised him, but You do not despise the little ones.

2.19.6.en: You took this little shepherd, and set him on the throne to shepherd Your people.

2.19.7.en: Instead of the flute that gathers the sheep around him, You made him the sweet psalmist of Israel.

2.19.8.en: v You chose his son Solomon as a king wise in his youth.

2.19.9.en: You gave him wisdom from on high.

2.19.10.en: And with wisdom You gave him riches, glory and a good name.

2.19.11.en: You put it in his heart to build You a house, O You whom the heavens and the earth cannot contain.

2.19.12.en: v You gave him wisdom, grace and good management.

2.19.13.en: He made the king of Tyre a partner in building Your holy house.

2.19.14.en: And he called the strangers to work for You, O Holy One.

2.19.15.en: He found favor in the eyes of all.

2.19.16.en: And in his wisdom he did not exploit their love, but provided them with their needs in return for their work.

2.19.17.en: v O You who chose David and Solomon, and gave each of them the work according to his gifts and abilities.

2.19.18.en: What, then, O Lord, do You want me to do?

2.19.19.en: Open my eyes, that I may realize what my mission is.

2.19.20.en: Hold my hand and lead me, that my depths may be strengthened.

2.19.21.en: So that I may work not in slackness and faintheartedness,

2.19.22.en: but through You I can do all things.

2.19.23.en: Grant me not to turn to the right or to the left,

2.19.24.en: but by Your Holy Spirit to hold to the royal road!

2.19.25.en: Be my leader, my helper and my refuge, so that I never cease to work according to Your holy will.
